one_liner: Ahead-of-time transpiler from implicitly statically typed Python 3 to C++; README claims 12x median over CPython 3.14.
what_it_does: Shed Skin infers static types for a whole Python program and emits C++ that links against its own C++ reimplementation of the builtins and about 33 partially supported stdlib modules. `shedskin build prog` produces a stand-alone executable; `shedskin build -e mod` produces a CPython extension module whose functions are called from ordinary Python. It is not a drop-in interpreter: code needs no annotations but must be monomorphic (one type per variable, homogeneous containers), avoid eval/getattr/isinstance, *args/**kwargs, nested functions, closures and multiple inheritance, and use no external libraries inside the compiled part.
how_it_is_fast: Whole-program type inference (rewritten in 0.9.14) lets every variable become a fixed C++ type, so ints and floats are unboxed machine values (int64 by default, int32 with --int32) and attribute access is a direct member access with no dictionary lookup or bytecode dispatch. Lists map to std::vector, dicts and sets to std::unordered_map/unordered_set (boost::unordered_flat_map/small_vector with --boost), all allocated through the Boehm GC's gc_allocator; idiomatic enumerate/zip/items loops have their temporary tuples optimized away. Optional flags strip Python safety checks: -b (bounds), -w (negative-index wrap), -z (zero division), plus --predict for run-time list-size prediction.
when_to_use: A self-contained CPU-bound kernel of a few hundred to a few thousand lines (simulations, search, ray tracers, emulators, compressors) that you want 10x+ faster without rewriting it in C++.
You want to keep CPython as the main interpreter and call the hot part as an extension module, passing scalars, builtin containers or instances of your own classes.
Code that is already effectively monomorphic and uses only builtins plus modules such as math, random, re, collections, heapq, itertools, array, struct.
You need a stand-alone native binary from Python source (linking only libgc and pcre2) rather than a bundled interpreter.
when_not_to_use: Programs that depend on numpy, third-party packages or unsupported stdlib modules inside the hot code; numpy arrays must be converted with tolist(), which the docs call very inefficient.
Code that relies on Python big integers, dict insertion order, isinstance/getattr or other dynamic features: ints are fixed-width and 'ordered dicts' are listed as unsupported.

Large code bases: the docs say type inference does not scale well beyond several thousand lines (largest compiled program about 6,000 lines), and open issue #1032 reports the same input taking 28 s or 500 s to analyse.
Hot paths that make many small calls across the extension-module boundary: builtin objects are fully converted (deep copy) on every call and return.
When you need full Python compatibility with little porting effort: PyPy, Nuitka or Cython run unmodified code; Shed Skin may require 'a lot' of refactoring per its README.

integration.dependencies: Boehm GC (libgc), PCRE2, Python development headers (for extension modules), CMake for the build/run subcommands; boost containers are bundled for --boost; Windows fetches C++ deps via CMake FetchContent
integration.min_toolchain: Python >= 3.8 to run the transpiler; C++20 compiler (g++ -std=c++20 on Linux/macOS, MSVC Build Tools on Windows); CMake 3.18.4+
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows (MSVC + CMake); platform-specific stdlib functionality unsupported
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the threading module is not in the supported list (multiprocessing over extension modules is the documented route to parallelism)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: only a restricted, implicitly statically typed Python subset compiles, usually after refactoring; compiled extension modules are imported like normal modules

gotchas: Integers are fixed-width C++ ints (int64 default since 0.9.13; the README sieve rows used --int32), not Python big ints; generated executables are built without -fwrapv, so overflow is C++ undefined behaviour (only extension modules get -fwrapv). None becomes a NULL pointer, so untested paths can segfault.

Semantics differ from CPython: dicts are std::unordered_map (iteration order not insertion order), function-argument evaluation order changes, and -w/--nowrap silently stops negative indices from wrapping (the 1.8 s sieve row used --nowrap --nobounds).

Build flags depend on the path: `shedskin translate` uses the FLAGS file (-O2 -march=native -DNDEBUG), while `shedskin build` on Unix hard-codes -O2 without -march=native; on Windows `build` passes `--config Debug` unless --build-type is given and the -O2 option is added only for UNIX, so default Windows binaries (build/Debug/test.exe) are unoptimized debug builds.

Harness flaw: the README sieve table says n=100000000, but examples/sieve/sieve.py hard-codes n = 10000000 at both tag v0.9.9 and HEAD (HEAD also runs main() 10 times and times only the last 5 for PyPy warm-up), so the published timings cannot be reproduced from the committed example; the 'benchmarked by asv' badge points to shedskin/benchmarks, a separate microtest suite with one 2015-era machine (Intel i5-3320M, Linux 4.0.6 fc22), not the 80-example 1-100x claim.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Shed Skin over Cython or mypyc when the code is unannotated but effectively monomorphic and you want a large speedup without writing type declarations, and over PyPy when you must stay on CPython and only a small kernel needs to be fast; prefer Codon for a broader Python-like language with its own compiler and runtime, and PyPy, Nuitka or Cython when the code uses dynamic features or third-party libraries.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README numbers: across the 80+ programs in examples/ the compiled code is 1-100x faster than CPython 3.14 (average 20x, median 12x), with no per-program table, script, CPU or compiler stated; a sieve run (labelled n=100000000) took 13.4 s on CPython 3.10.6, 11.4 s on 3.11.0, 5.8 s on PyPy 3.9 and 1.9 s on Shed Skin 0.9.9 with --int32 (1.8 s adding --nowrap --nobounds), about 6-7x (derived from page data) on unstated hardware.
status_note: Actively maintained (0.9.14 with a type-inference rewrite and Unicode str, last commit 2026-10-05, about 1.0k stars, 106 open issues); the GPL-3.0 compiler does not cover generated programs' runtime, which is Expat/BSD-3/BSL-1.0, so output is copyable, but the docs still call it experimental.
